newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada confirms key element in Nazi gold saga.
newsitem.headline: Canada confirms key element in Nazi gold saga.

text.p: The Bank of Canada confirmed on Monday key elements of a U.S. war-time intelligence document that appeared to show how Portugal managed to launder looted gold it had bought from the Nazis during the Second World War.

"The Bank of Canada transactions in question, which were described in the recently released U.S. government documents, have been readily verified from ledgers, and related correspondence has been examined," the central bank reported.

Portugal was officially neutral during the war but the U.S. documents, dated Sept. 10, 1944, said that in 1942 the Bank of Portugal deposited four tons of gold it had bought from Nazi Germany in its account with the Swiss National Bank.
The Swiss, it said, transferred the same amount of gold it had in a Bank of Canada account to the Portuguese, who, in turn, transferred title to the gold in its Swiss account.

The document was released on July 10 by the World Jewish Congress, prompting an official search in Canada and other countries to see whether they may have, perhaps unwittingly and indirectly, helped the Nazis unload gold they had looted.
The Bank of Canada stressed that it had no records of physically receiving gold from Switzerland or Portugal nor of shipping gold to those countries during the war.

"There is no evidence in our review to date of any such transactions and also no evidence that gold bars looted in Europe by the Nazis ended up in vaults of the Bank of Canada," it said in Monday's interim report.
But it documented how at the start of the war Britain had deposited 2,154 tons of gold for wartime safekeeping at the Bank of Canada in Ottawa.

Starting in March 1942 the Bank of England transferred ownership of 56 tons of British gold to the account of the Swiss central bank in exchange for Swiss francs provided to the British for the war effort. Canada's Department of Finance approved this, along with restrictions on its transfer.

In the following six weeks, at the request of the Swiss central bank, the Bank of Canada transferred ownership of four tons of gold from the account of the Swiss National Bank to that of the Bank of Portugal, with the same restrictions.
The Bank of Canada acted on a similar request on Sept. 19, 1944, to transfer two tons of gold from the Swiss account to the Portuguese account.
On Sept. 7 and Oct. 2, 1944, it transferred 1.5 tons from the Portuguese account to that of the central bank of Sweden, another neutral country to which a transfer was allowed.

The U.S. document said the Portuguese objective was "to get rid of gold purchased from the Reichsbank through the Banque Nationale Suisse (Swiss National Bank)," and said 15 tons were swapped through the Federal Reserve Bank in New York in 1944.
